# Week 5, Day 4.1 - Prerequisites check

Today every page class becomes a fixture. That needs one type-level tool you have not used yet.

| Concept | Taught in |
|---|---|
| `test.extend` with fixtures | [week3/day3_3](/learn/w3/d3/p3) |
| Classes, `extends` | [day3_1](/learn/w5/d3/p1) |
| A `type` alias for an object | new - below |
| Re-exporting (`export { x }`) | new - below |
| Dynamic `import()` | new - below |

**Next:** [Day 4.2 - Composing page objects](/learn/w5/d4/p2)

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Concept 2 - re-exporting

A spec should need one import line, not two. A fixtures module can pass `expect` straight
through:

```ts
import { test as base, expect } from "@playwright/test";
export const test = base.extend<Pages>({ ... });
export { expect };                       // <- re-export, unchanged
```

Now `import { test, expect } from "./pages/test";` is the whole import block.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Concept 3 - dynamic `import()`

A normal `import` sits at the top of a file. `await import(...)` fetches a module *where you
stand*, and returns a promise for its exports.

| Form | Runs | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `import { x } from "m"` | at load | almost always |
| `const { x } = await import("m")` | when reached | something needed by one test only |

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.
**Next:** [Day 4.2 - Composing page objects](/learn/w5/d4/p2)

## Step 1 - a third page class

`TransferPage` covers the screen behind the Add Payee tile.

## Step 2 - each page becomes a fixture

One module, one job: hand out page objects on request.

Three things happening there:

| Line | Does |
|---|---|
| `type Pages = { loginPage: LoginPage; ... }` | names what each fixture hands you |
| `base.extend<Pages>({ ... })` | adds them to the `test` function |
| `export { expect }` | so a spec needs one import line, not two |

And the property that makes it worth doing: **a test that does not ask for `transferPage` never
constructs one.** Fixtures are lazy - Playwright runs the function only when a test names it in
its parameter list.

## Step 3 - the spec

Note the import: `from "./pages/test"`, not from `@playwright/test`. That is the only change a
spec file needs.

## Step 4 - count the DOM details in that file

Zero. No placeholders, no button names, no CSS, no URLs except in `expect(page).toHaveURL(...)` -
and that is an assertion about *behaviour*, which belongs in the test.

Every line says what a person did or what should be true. That is the finish line for this
pattern.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Step 6 - a fixture that signs you in

The next step most teams take: a fixture that *does* something, not just constructs.

```ts
signedIn: async ({ loginPage, dashboardPage }, use) => {
  await loginPage.goto("/");
  await loginPage.signIn();
  await use(dashboardPage);       // hand the test a dashboard, already signed in
},
```

A fixture can depend on other fixtures. Everything before `use()` is setup, everything after is
teardown - and a test that asks for `signedIn` gets the sign-in without writing it.

| Compared with | Difference |
|---|---|
| `beforeEach` | a fixture is opt-in per test; a hook applies to every test in the block |
| `storageState` ([day2_2](/learn/w5/d2/p2)) | still a real UI sign-in, so it is slower but tests the form |

parts.title: How a real repo scales it

blocks.text:
# Week 5, Day 4.3 - How a real repo scales it

Same `test.extend`, same page classes - at 300 tests.

## The fixtures file is a bottleneck

Every spec imports it, so every page class it names gets loaded - even for a test that uses one.
Two ways teams handle it:

| Approach | Trade |
|---|---|
| One `fixtures/test.ts` with every page | simplest; slowest to load, and one merge-conflict hotspot |
| One fixtures file per area, all extending a shared base | more files, no hotspot |

Splitting by area:

```ts
// fixtures/base.ts        - things every area needs
export const test = base.extend<Core>({ ... });

// fixtures/payments.ts    - extends it again
import { test as coreTest } from "./base";
export const test = coreTest.extend<PaymentPages>({ ... });
```

`extend` returns a new `test`, so chaining is the intended use.

`testB.cart` is empty because a test-scoped fixture is rebuilt each time. The token is not - and
anything mutable held at worker scope is a channel between tests, which is the same trap as the
shared account in [day2_2](/learn/w5/d2/p2).

## What actually keeps a big POM suite alive

| Practice | Why |
|---|---|
| One class per page, one file per class | you can find things by name |
| Inheritance one level deep; compose the rest | see [day3_3](/learn/w5/d3/p3) |
| No `expect` in `pages/` | rule 3 |
| Fixtures for construction, not for logic | a fixture doing five things is a hidden `beforeEach` |
| A lint rule banning raw selectors in `specs/` | catches the hole before review does |

**Next:** [Day 4.4 - Practice](/learn/w5/d4/p4)

# Week 5, Day 4.4 - Practice

Work in `week5/generated/`. Copy `pages/test.ts` to `pages/mytest.ts` and extend that, so the
Day 4.2 cells keep running.
**Next:** [Day 5.1 - Prerequisites](/learn/w5/d5/p1)

problems.statement:
**Add a fixture**
Add your `PayBillsPage` from Day 3.4 to a copy of the fixtures module, and use it in a spec.

**Right when:** the spec never writes `new`, and passes.

**Prove fixtures are lazy**
Add `console.log("constructing TransferPage")` to that fixture. Run a test that does *not* ask
for it.

**Right when:** the line does not appear - and appears as soon as a test names the fixture.

**A signedIn fixture**
Write the `signedIn` fixture from Day 4.2 Step 6. Use it to rewrite two tests.

**Right when:** both pass and neither mentions `signIn()`.

**Fixture versus beforeEach**
Keep two versions of the same two tests: one using `signedIn`, one using a `beforeEach`.

**Right when:** you can state one thing the fixture gives you that the hook cannot. (Hint: add a
third test that must run signed *out*.)

**A worker fixture**
Write a worker-scoped fixture that logs a random number once, and four tests that print it.

**Right when:** with `--workers=1` all four print the same number; with `--workers=4` you can
explain the pattern you see.

**An auto fixture that fails the run**
Write the `failOnConsoleError` fixture from Day 4.3. Then add a test that triggers a console
error with `page.evaluate(() => console.error("boom"))`.

**Right when:** that test fails, no other test does, and no test file mentions the fixture.

**Find the leak**
Write a worker fixture holding a mutable array. Have test A push to it and test B assert it is
empty. Run with `--workers=1`, then `--workers=2`.

**Right when:** the result changes with the worker count, and you can explain why this is the
same bug as the shared account in [day2_2](/learn/w5/d2/p2).
